words.etymon: unmapped (Celtic *knu-; not cognate with Latv. rieksts)

cognate: OIr. áirne 'sloe' ~ Latv. oga 'berry' (*h₂og-/*ōg-; Lith. úoga, OCS (j)agoda); OIr. uball ~ Latv. ābols (*h₂ébōl); both are north-western (Celtic-Germanic-Balto-Slavic) lexemes
drift_or_renewal: 'nut' slot renewed (OIr. cnú vs Latv. rieksts, not cognate); the berry term is specialised to 'sloe' in Irish, general 'berry' in Latvian
shared_syntax: Only partly shared: both are coordinated lists of the same three noun classes (nut, berry/sloe, apple) at one syntactic level, but the frames differ: Irish is a negated litany (nī X ocus nī Y), Latvian a purposive list with pa + dative/instrumental ('after berries, after nuts, after sour apples')
context: Both lists name the wild fruit gathered from forest trees and bushes: the Irish poem denies that its subject is nut, brown berry, sloe or apple; the daina has the forester's daughter going out day after day for berries, nuts and (wild) sour apples. In Irish the triad is fixed rather than ad hoc: it recurs in Old Irish as 'cnú is áirne is uball', and in annals and lore as the mast of trees (cnoa, dercna, ubla). Against inheritance: these are simply the three obvious wild fruits of temperate Europe, so any forager's list in any language will name them; both witnesses are late (Early Modern Irish, a daina quoted in OCR); the pivot is research-only; there is only one Baltic witness, because the Latvian dainas corpus lies under off-limits raw/books and the Lithuanian dainos gave no co-occurrence. At best a shared inventory of cognate items in a list, not a demonstrable formula
phrase: 'nut(s), berry/sloe, apple(s)' as the coordinated triad of wild forest fruit

note: All 168 bundles read (all pivots are Early Modern Irish, mostly the Imtheachta Aeniasa and Togail na Tebe translations, Bevis/Guy of Warwick, a herbal and bardic verse; partners are mostly Greek prose). One low claim (BC-0420d, a fruit triad). Dropped BC-2a92e (muir/tír ~ Lucretius mare/terris): the Irish renders Aen. 6.692 terras...aequora, so it is a translation, and the Latin partner is physics prose, not a merism. Other translational echoes (BC-dd722 'a hundred tongues, an iron voice' = Aen. 6.625; BC-45bbd river red with blood, plains white with bones = Aen. 12.35-36) have no congruent partner and are Vergilian, not inherited.
